1051.title: the summit sit
1051.hook: a lotus leaf sits in the pond all day, and the water rolls off it in beads
1051.howItsDone: The paths of karma, bhakti and jnana are walked side by side and in combination: selfless work and service, devotion in worship and kirtan, and study and inquiry with a teacher; the Gita is read as holding all three.

segments.voice: Yesterday the summit sit went back to the modern teachers, and Ramana's question: to whom did this thought come? Did a worry get asked that question? Today, the three tracks. Day one thousand fifty-one.

Rain falls on a pond. The water gathers on a lotus leaf in bright beads, rolls to the edge, and slides off. The leaf has been in the water all its life. It isn't wet. The Bhagavad Gita uses that leaf in its fifth chapter, as a picture of a person who acts fully in the world and isn't stained by it. That chapter sat inside the lineage weeks of this year, when the path split into three tracks: karma, bhakti and jnana. Today's summit sit climbs back to those weeks.
screen: `WATER ON A LOTUS LEAF.` → `IN THE POND, NOT WET.` → `THE THREE TRACKS.`

segments.voice: Here is the Gita's line, in paraphrase, from chapter five: one who acts while placing every action in Brahman, letting go of clinging, is not touched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is not touched by water. Hold that leaf up and look at it from each of the year's three tracks. On the karma track, we read Gita chapters three, four and five, and designed a year of service. There the leaf means doing the work well and setting down the result. Act, and don't grip the outcome. On the bhakti track, we read the Gita Govinda and the Bhagavata's tenth book, and sang kirtan. There the leaf turns into an offering. Elsewhere the Gita has Krishna say, in paraphrase: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, do it as an offering to me. The act is the same. Now it is a gift. On the jnana track, we read Shankara's Crest-Jewel of Discrimination and the Ashtavakra Gita. There the leaf is the witness. Ashtavakra tells King Janaka, in paraphrase: you are not the earth, not water, not fire, not air, not space; know yourself as the witness of all these. The water rolls by; the one who sees it was never wet. Three tracks, three readings of one leaf. And the Gita itself, in the same chapter, says that only the childish call the path of knowledge and the path of action different; the one who truly stands in either reaches the fruit of both. Read that way, the tracks aren't a contest. They're three ways up.
screen: `NOT TOUCHED, LIKE A LOTUS LEAF.` · `KARMA: SET DOWN THE RESULT.` · `BHAKTI: MAKE IT AN OFFERING.` · `JNANA: THE WITNESS, NEVER WET.` · then, large: `THREE WAYS UP.`

segments.voice: Sit for the bell's two minutes, and bring to mind one ordinary task from today: a dish, an email, a drive. Hold it for a few breaths the karma way: do it well, and let the result go. Then the bhakti way: if you pray, see it as something offered. Then the jnana way: notice the one who watches the task being done, still and dry, like the leaf. Don't pick a favorite. Let each one have a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the lineage tracks of karma, bhakti and jnana, and the lotus leaf in the pond.
Your line: the summit sit. Today, finish one task and then lift your hands off it for a moment, like water sliding from a lotus leaf. Day one thousand fifty-one.

options: hold on tight until the result comes in.
act fully, then let the result roll off, like water on a leaf.
next time, don't act at all.
fork.reveal: the Gita pictures someone who acts, places the action in Brahman and lets go of clinging, untouched as a lotus leaf by water. it never says to stop acting.

what it means: the year's three tracks read the same Gita, and the Gita says the wise see knowledge and action as one.

1052.title: the summit sit
1052.hook: a shelf holds a string of beads, a candle stub, a folded blanket and a card of Sanskrit letters
1052.howItsDone: Practitioners often keep a daily sadhana, a regular personal practice that may combine breathwork, japa on a mala, a gaze or a mudra, and quiet sitting, ideally at the same time each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday the summit sit went back to the three tracks, and the lotus leaf that sits in the water and stays dry. Did you lift your hands off one finished task? Today, the practices. Day one thousand fifty-two.

A string of beads, worn smooth in one spot. A candle burned down to a stub. A blanket, folded, that someone lay under with their eyes closed. A card with Sanskrit letters on it, the vowels first. Put them on one shelf and you have the last block of practice from this year: breath, mantra, rest, gaze, hands and sound. Today's summit sit climbs back to that shelf, and instead of talking about the practices, it does a little of each.
screen: `BEADS, A CANDLE, A BLANKET, A CARD.` → `ONE SHELF.` → `THE PRACTICES, DEEPER.`

segments.voice: First, the shelf by name. Pranayama sequences: shaping the breath. Mantra sadhana: a sacred sound repeated on the beads, day after day. Yoga nidra: lying still and letting the body be scanned and released while awareness stays awake. Trataka: a still gaze on one small point. The mudras: the hands held in a shape that means something. And Sanskrit sounds: the alphabet heard before it is read. Six practices. Looked at from the top, they share one direction. Each takes something that usually runs on its own, the breath, the tongue, the body, the eyes, the hands, the voice, and asks it to do one thing on purpose for a while. The Yoga Sutra has a short line about what makes any practice hold. In paraphrase: practice becomes firmly grounded when it's kept up for a long time, without breaks, and with care. Long, unbroken, and with care. Notice what that line doesn't ask for. It doesn't ask for hard, or impressive, or perfect. The word for this kind of steady practice, the word that sits behind this whole block, is sadhana. A sadhana is the practice you return to, the one that becomes yours by being done. The beads get smooth in one spot because the same fingers keep coming back. So today the summit sit isn't a review in words. It's a short sadhana that borrows one breath from each part of the shelf.
screen: `SIX PRACTICES ON ONE SHELF.` · `EACH ASKS ONE THING, ON PURPOSE.` · `LONG, UNBROKEN, WITH CARE.` · `SADHANA: THE PRACTICE YOU RETURN TO.` · then, large: `A LITTLE OF EACH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let one breath out run a little longer than the breath in. Rest the thumb and first finger of each hand together, the others relaxed. Let your eyes find one small point in front of you and stay there gently, blinking when you need to. Then let them close. If you keep a mantra, let it move quietly with the breath. If not, the open sound, ah, said silently. Feel the body grow heavy where it touches the floor or chair, and keep the watcher awake. Stay with all of it, lightly. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the practices, gathered into a single sit, a little of each.
Your line: the summit sit. Today, pick the one practice from that shelf you'd most like to keep, and give it one minute before bed. Day one thousand fifty-two.

options: the hardest one, done once a month.
whichever one, kept up long, without breaks, with care.

fork.reveal: the sutra names three conditions: a long time, no breaks, and care. it says nothing about difficulty.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sadhana, a steady spiritual practice, the one you return to.

trapdoor: what you thought: deeper practice means harder practice.
what it means: a sadhana deepens by being kept up long, without breaks, and with care.
what a scholar hears: Yoga Sutra 1.14, dirgha-kala, nairantarya, satkara: long time, without interruption, with devotion.

1053.title: the summit sit
1053.hook: at the end of the Gita, the charioteer who heard it all keeps remembering it, and rejoices again and again
1053.howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita is recited and heard in whole or in part, and a full recitation ends with these closing verses; the epics and Puranas are counted among the smriti, the remembered texts.

segments.voice: Yesterday the summit sit gathered the practices into one short sadhana: a breath, the hands, a gaze, a sound. Which one did you give a minute to last night? Today the week of summit sits closes. Day one thousand fifty-three.

The Bhagavad Gita doesn't end with Krishna's last word. It ends with two people remembering. Arjuna speaks once more, briefly, and then the voice goes back to Sanjaya, the king's charioteer, who has been describing the whole conversation from far away. Sanjaya says that as he remembers this dialogue, he rejoices, again and again. And as he remembers that form of Krishna, he is amazed, and rejoices again. Remembering, and rejoicing again. That's a good place to finish a week of summit sits.
screen: `THE GITA ENDS IN MEMORY.` → `SANJAYA REMEMBERS.` → `AND REJOICES, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Listen to what Arjuna actually says, near the close of the eighteenth chapter, in paraphrase: my confusion is gone. Through your grace I have regained memory. I stand firm, my doubts are scattered. I will do as you say. He doesn't say he has learned something new. He says memory has come back. The word there is smriti, memory, and it carries weight in this tradition. It's also the name given to the great body of remembered texts, the epics and the Puranas among them, books this year often read from. So look at this week from the top. The first sit went back to the great story, and a king who would not leave a dog on the mountain. The second to Krishna's childhood, and a mother who saw the universe in her son's mouth and was given back her son. The third to the saints of bhakti, singing in the language of home. The fourth to the modern teachers, and Ramana's question, who am I? The fifth to the three tracks, and a lotus leaf that stays dry in the pond. The sixth to the practices, a little of each. None of it was new. All of it was remembered. Read that way, Arjuna's line makes remembering no lesser thing than learning: in his case, the moment the confusion clears is a moment of memory. Sanjaya models the next step. He doesn't just remember once. He keeps returning to it, and keeps being glad. That's what a summit sit is for. Climb up, look back over the way you came, and go over it again, glad, the way Sanjaya did.
screen: `I HAVE REGAINED MEMORY.` · `SMRITI: THE REMEMBERED TEXTS.` · `SIX SITS, ALL REMEMBERED.` · `RETURN, AND REJOICE AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WAY, AS ONE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Sit for the bell's two minutes. Let the week walk back through you, one picture for each sit: a dog on a mountain road. A child's open mouth. A weaver singing at a loom. A question: who am I? Water rolling off a leaf. Beads worn smooth. Give each one a breath. Then let them go, and sit with whatever stays. If one of them makes you glad, let yourself be glad again, the way Sanjaya was. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. A week of sitting at the top of the year and looking back, stretch by stretch. Today, the week itself, held in memory, the way the Gita ends.
Your line: the summit sit. Today, return once to a memory from this year that made you glad, and let it make you glad again. Day one thousand fifty-three.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: smriti, memory; also the name for the remembered texts, including the epics.

1054.title: the ranges ahead
1054.hook: beaten gods pour out their light, and the light becomes a goddess
1054.howItsDone: The Devi Mahatmya is recited in homes and temples, especially during Navaratri, the goddess's festival; the scene of her forming from the gods' light is painted, sung and acted out.

segments.voice: Last week closed with the summit sit, and Sanjaya remembering the Gita and rejoicing again and again. Did a glad memory come back to you? A new week, the last of the year. Now we turn and look forward. Day one thousand fifty-four.

Year three on this path was the great story and the saints. Year four has a name too: the schools and the goddess. From the summit, the next ranges are already in view, and this week takes a first look at them, one ridge at a time. The first ridge opens with a scene. The gods have lost. A buffalo demon, Mahisha, has driven them out of heaven. Led by Brahma, they go to Shiva and Vishnu and tell them everything. And the three great gods, hearing it, grow so angry that light begins to pour out of their faces.
screen: `THE SCHOOLS AND THE GODDESS.` → `THE GODS HAVE LOST.` → `LIGHT POURS FROM THEIR FACES.`

segments.voice: That scene is from the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, and it's where year four begins. In its second episode, in paraphrase, a great blaze of light streams from Vishnu, from Shiva, from Brahma, and then from all the other gods as well. The light gathers into one mass, like a burning mountain filling the sky. And the mass takes form as a woman. Then each god gives her something of his own. Shiva draws a trident out of his trident and hands it to her. Vishnu brings forth a discus from his discus. One by one, the others give. She laughs, and the world shakes, and she goes out to meet Mahisha. Look at what the story is saying in its own way. The goddess isn't presented as a helper sent by one god. She's what appears when every power is gathered into one, and she is the one who can act when the gods themselves couldn't. The tradition's word for that power is shakti. Year four opens with her: the Devi Mahatmya read whole; Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati and Parvati as characters; shakti as a way of thinking about the world; hymns to the goddess; and Navaratri, the goddess's festival, as a curriculum. And that's only the first ridge. Beyond it, Shiva, the schools of thought, the Vedas, the women of the epics, regional traditions. This week, we'll look at a few of them from here. Not to climb them yet. Just to know their shape.
screen: `THE GLORY OF THE GODDESS.` · `EVERY GOD'S LIGHT, GATHERED INTO ONE.` · `EACH GOD GIVES A WEAPON.` · `SHAKTI: THE POWER THAT ACTS.` · then, large: `THE FIRST RIDGE OF YEAR FOUR.`

segments.voice: Sit for the bell's two minutes. Notice where your energy is scattered right now: a little in a worry, a little in a plan, a little in a screen across the room. Don't scold any of it. Just, breath by breath, invite each scattered piece to come home, the way the light of every god gathered into one. Let it gather somewhere near the center of the chest. When it scatters again, gather it again. The bell holds the time.
The ranges ahead. From the top of year three, a first look at year four. Today's ridge: the goddess, made of every god's light gathered into one.
Your line: the ranges ahead. Today, once, when you feel pulled in several directions, stop and gather yourself into one thing for one minute. Day one thousand fifty-four.

1055.title: the ranges ahead
1055.hook: a hungry hunter waits all night in a tree, and the leaves he drops land somewhere he can't see
1055.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, devotees fast, keep vigil through the night, chant to Shiva, and offer water, milk and bilva leaves on the Shiva linga, and the story of the hunter is often retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ranges ahead, and the first ridge of year four: the goddess, made of every god's light gathered into one. Did you gather yourself into one thing for a minute? Today, the next ridge. Day one thousand fifty-five.

A hunter has caught nothing all day, and his family is waiting for food. Night comes. He climbs a tree beside a pool, where animals will come to drink, and settles in with his bow. He's cold. He's hungry. He can't let himself sleep. So his hands stay busy: he plucks leaves from the branches and lets them fall, one after another, into the dark below. He has no idea what's down there. That story is told in the Shiva Purana, and retold on one particular night of the year. It's the gate to the second ridge ahead.
screen: `A HUNTER, EMPTY-HANDED.` → `ALL NIGHT IN A TREE.` → `LEAVES FALLING IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here is the turn, in paraphrase. The tree is a bilva tree, whose leaves are offered to Shiva. And at its foot, unseen in the dark, stands a Shiva linga. All night long, the hunter's restless leaves fall onto it, along with drops of water. He stays awake through every watch of the night. It is Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, though he doesn't know it. When deer come to the water, he draws his bow, and each time he ends up letting them go. By morning, the story says, his heart has changed, and Shiva appears to him. He fasted because he had no food. He kept vigil because he was afraid to sleep. He worshipped because his hands were fidgeting. The story is gentle about it. Shiva accepted the night anyway. That's a fair picture of the second range in year four. After the goddess comes Shiva. The Shiva Purana, in selections. Nataraja, the dancing form, explained piece by piece. The Shiva Sahasranama, a hymn of his names, in selections. The Rudram, a Vedic hymn chanted to him. A first look at Kashmir Shaivism and its Shiva Sutras. And Maha Shivaratri itself, taught as a night-long curriculum, watch by watch, the way the hunter kept it without meaning to. Even from here, some of its forms stand out: the dancer, the ascetic on the mountain, the householder with Parvati, the one who drank poison to save the world. Today, only its outline from far away.
screen: `A BILVA TREE, A HIDDEN LINGA.` · `A VIGIL KEPT WITHOUT KNOWING.` · `SHIVA ACCEPTS THE NIGHT.` · `THE SECOND RIDGE: SHIVA.` · then, large: `THE DANCER AND THE ASCETIC.`

segments.voice: Sit for the bell's two minutes, as if it were a short watch of the night. Let your hands rest open on your knees. Each time you breathe out, picture one leaf leaving your hand and falling into the dark, onto something you can't see. You don't need to know where it lands. Let each breath out be that kind of small offering, given without checking. If you're tired, that's fine. The hunter was too. The bell holds the time.
The ranges ahead. From the top of year three, a look at year four. Today's ridge: Shiva, and a night kept by a hunter who didn't know it was holy.
Your line: the ranges ahead. Today, do one small kind thing without checking whether anyone saw it or where it landed. Day one thousand fifty-five.

1056.title: the ranges ahead
1056.hook: a queen in a gambling hall asks a question the elders in the room cannot settle, and a poet in the hills answers in her own voice
1056.howItsDone: Akka Mahadevi's vachanas are sung and recited in Karnataka, Lal Ded's sayings are quoted in Kashmir, and the women of the epics are honored in stories, songs and festivals across India.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ranges ahead, and Shiva's ridge, with a hunter who kept a holy night without knowing it. Did a small kindness land somewhere you didn't check? Today, another ridge. Day one thousand fifty-six.
screen: `THE RANGES AHEAD.` · `A NIGHT KEPT WITHOUT KNOWING.`

segments.voice: This year, in the dice game, Draupadi was dragged into a hall full of men and asked them a question. Had her husband lost himself before he staked her? If he had, was she his to lose? Bhishma answered that the way of dharma was too subtle for him to decide. Young Vikarna spoke up for her and was shouted down. The question hung in the air of the Mahabharata and never quite came down. Draupadi's voice reaches us inside a vast story told about her. There are also women in this tradition who left their own words behind, poems and sayings in their own voices. A season of them waits in year four. That's today's ridge.
screen: `DRAUPADI'S QUESTION.` → `THE ELDERS CAN'T SETTLE IT.` → `WOMEN, IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: The plan for that season is simple to say. The tradition's women, from the epics and from the saints: Sita, Draupadi, Kunti, Gandhari, Savitri, Damayanti, Shakuntala, and then Andal, Mirabai, Akka Mahadevi and Lal Ded. And wherever they left words of their own, those words, not only words about them. Two of those names, Akka and Lalla, haven't come up on this path yet, so here's a first look. Akka Mahadevi sang in Kannada, in short free poems called vachanas, sayings. Again and again her poems speak to one beloved, her name for Shiva: Chennamallikarjuna, the lord white as jasmine. The story told about her says she left her home and walked out into the world to find him, covered only by her own long hair. Some readers hear her poems as blunt and tender at once: a woman telling God, plainly, that she will have no other. Far to the north, in Kashmir, Lal Ded, also called Lalla, left sayings in Kashmiri. In one saying attributed to her, in paraphrase, she tells how she wandered far, searching, and found what she was looking for at home, inside. Look at the range from here. In the epics, women like Draupadi, Kunti and Gandhari stand at some of the story's hardest turns and say the thing no one wants said. In the saints, women like Andal, Mira, Akka and Lalla speak about God in the first person, in their own languages. Year four sets those voices side by side. Not as a special topic. As part of the main road.
screen: `FROM THE EPICS AND THE SAINTS.` · `AKKA: THE LORD WHITE AS JASMINE.` · `LALLA: SEARCHED FAR, FOUND AT HOME.` · `THE HARDEST TURNS, THE FIRST PERSON.` · then, large: `PART OF THE MAIN ROAD.`

segments.voice: Sit for the bell's two minutes. Bring to mind a woman whose voice shaped yours: a mother, a grandmother, a teacher, an aunt, a friend. Not what people said about her. Something she herself said, a phrase you can still hear in her tone. Let it come back in her voice. Rest with it for a few breaths. If more of her words come, let them. If only one, that's enough. The bell holds the time.
The ranges ahead. From the top of year three, a look at year four. Today's ridge: the women of the tradition, heard in their own words wherever their words survive.
Your line: the ranges ahead. Today, ask a woman in your life about something she believes or remembers, and listen to it in her own words. Day one thousand fifty-six.

1057.title: the ranges ahead
1057.hook: a child on a rooftop asks what was there before everything, and a hymn ahead on the path asks it too
1057.howItsDone: Hymns of the Rig Veda are still recited and chanted, in traditional recitation by memory, and some readers, Hindu and not, turn to the Nasadiya Sukta as a hymn that leaves the question of creation open.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ranges ahead, and the women who left words in their own voices: Akka Mahadevi and Lal Ded. Did you ask a woman in your life what she believes or remembers, and hear it in her words? Day one thousand fifty-seven.
screen: `THE RANGES AHEAD.` · `WOMEN, IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: A summer night on a flat roof. A child lies on a mat, staring up, and asks the question that stops a bedtime cold: what was there before everything? Before the stars. Before the first morning. Before anything at all. The grown-up beside her starts an answer, and then the answer runs out, and the two of them just lie there looking up. Somewhere ahead on this path there's a hymn that asks that same question. It was sung, not whispered on a roof, and it was kept and carried as scripture. And it doesn't pretend to finish the answer either. Today, one of the ranges ahead: the Vedas themselves, and a hymn that ends with a question.
screen: `WHAT WAS THERE BEFORE EVERYTHING?` → `THE ANSWER RUNS OUT.` → `A HYMN THAT ASKS IT TOO.`

segments.voice: Next year the path climbs into the Vedas themselves. The word can sound like a rulebook. But the Rig Veda is a collection of hymns: songs of praise to Agni, the fire, to Ushas, the dawn, to Indra and to Varuna. Among them is a short hymn people call the Nasadiya Sukta, named from its opening words, and sometimes called the hymn of creation. In paraphrase, it begins: then there was neither what is nor what is not. No air, and no sky beyond it. Darkness, hidden in darkness. Then something stirs: a oneness, breathing without wind, and desire, which the hymn calls the first seed of mind. And then the hymn turns. Who truly knows? Who here could say where this creation came from? Even the gods, it says, came later than this making, so who knows where it arose? Then comes its last line. The one who watches over it all from the highest heaven surely knows. Or perhaps that one does not know. A hymn, kept as scripture, that ends with or perhaps not. That's worth carrying up a mountain. Last week was spent on the summit, looking back over the year. This week turned around to face what's still ahead, and the ranges from here are high. Nobody walks into them already knowing what's at the top. The Nasadiya Sukta suggests that's an honest way to begin. The question can stay open, and the path can still go on.
screen: `THE RIG VEDA: A COLLECTION OF HYMNS.` · `DARKNESS HIDDEN IN DARKNESS.` · `WHO TRULY KNOWS WHERE THIS CAME FROM?` · `OR PERHAPS THAT ONE DOES NOT KNOW.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION CAN STAY OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a question you can't answer. Settle, and let the breath come and go on its own. Then, quietly, ask the hymn's question: before all this, what was there? Don't reach for an answer. Let the question stay in the room, the way the child's did on the roof. When the mind hurries to fill it, come back to the breath, which arrived before you asked for it. If you pray, you can rest in front of God, or the gods, with the question still open. If you don't, simply sit beside it. The bell holds the time.
The ranges ahead. The years of the path still to climb. Among them, the Vedas themselves, where one hymn about the beginning of everything ends with or perhaps not.
Your line: the ranges ahead. Today, when someone asks you something you can't answer, try saying I don't know yet, and let it be a good question instead of a failure. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

fork.setup: you're singing a hymn about the beginning of everything, and you've reached the last line. how does it end?
options: name the maker and close the case.
say the watcher in highest heaven knows, or perhaps does not.
skip the question and praise the dawn instead.
fork.reveal: the Nasadiya Sukta ends with or perhaps that one does not know. a hymn kept as scripture leaves its own question open.

original.note: Sanskrit: the Nasadiya Sukta, named from its opening, 'then there was not non-being.' Rig Veda 10.129.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Vedas are a list of rules from the distant past.
what it means: the Rig Veda is hymns, and one of them, about the beginning of everything, ends with a question.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 10.129, nāsad āsīt, closing with so aṅga veda yadi vā na veda, 'that one surely knows, or perhaps does not know.'
